category: Adjectives with a to-infinitive or that-clause

examples: The first test was pretty easy.
This camera is easy to use, even for kids.
It's easier to take the subway than to find parking.
She has an easy, friendly way with customers.
We walked at an easy pace along the beach.
The two of them fell into an easy silence.
The coach was easy on the new players at first.
Her grandparents are much easier on her than her parents are.
Mr. Alvarez is an easy grader.
The new font is much easier on the eyes.
The lunch menu is easy on the wallet.

senses.head: Not difficult; done or understood without much effort
examples: The first test was pretty easy.
This camera is easy to use, even for kids.
It's easier to take the subway than to find parking.

senses.head: Relaxed and comfortable; free from worry or stiffness
examples: She has an easy, friendly way with customers.
We walked at an easy pace along the beach.
The two of them fell into an easy silence.

senses.head: easy on + person, or before a noun: not strict; not demanding much
examples: The coach was easy on the new players at first.
Her grandparents are much easier on her than her parents are.
Mr. Alvarez is an easy grader.

senses.head: easy on + the eyes, ears, stomach or budget: pleasant, not harsh or costly
examples: The new font is much easier on the eyes.
The lunch menu is easy on the wallet.

entries.takes: to-infinitive, where the subject is what you act on (easy to use, easy to talk to); for + person (easy for me); on + person (not strict) or + thing (pleasant for: easy on the eyes)
entries.contrast: Russian мне легко is It's easy for me, never I am easy. In This app is easy to use the subject is the thing you use, so He is easy to talk to means people find it easy to talk to him. The adverb is easily (She won easily), but fixed phrases keep easy: take it easy, go easy on him, easier said than done, easy come, easy go. Said of a woman, easy is an insulting old slang word for 'promiscuous'; the compliment for a relaxed person is easygoing.

examples: It's hard to believe she's only twelve.
The hardest part was waiting for the results.
That's a hard question to answer.
The mattress in the hotel was too hard.
Let the caramel cool until it's hard.
Diamonds are harder than any other natural material.
Moving furniture is hard work.
She's the hardest worker on the team.
After a hard day at the office, I just want to sleep.
Times were hard during the Great Depression.
It was the hardest winter the town had seen in decades.
He's had a hard life.
Don't be so hard on yourself.
Her father was a hard man who rarely smiled.
She gave him a hard look and said nothing.
He gave the door a hard push.
She took a hard fall on the ice.
The police have no hard evidence against him.
We need hard numbers, not guesses.
The bar serves beer and wine but no hard liquor.
He never touched hard drugs.
The water here is so hard it leaves spots on the glasses.
Hard water can damage your pipes over time.

senses.head: Difficult to do, understand or deal with
examples: It's hard to believe she's only twelve.
The hardest part was waiting for the results.
That's a hard question to answer.

senses.head: Solid and firm; not easy to bend, cut or press
examples: The mattress in the hotel was too hard.
Let the caramel cool until it's hard.
Diamonds are harder than any other natural material.

senses.head: Needing or using a lot of effort or energy
examples: Moving furniture is hard work.
She's the hardest worker on the team.
After a hard day at the office, I just want to sleep.

senses.head: Full of problems and suffering; harsh
examples: Times were hard during the Great Depression.
It was the hardest winter the town had seen in decades.
He's had a hard life.

senses.head: Strict, severe or unfriendly
examples: Don't be so hard on yourself.
Her father was a hard man who rarely smiled.
She gave him a hard look and said nothing.

senses.head: Done with a lot of force
examples: He gave the door a hard push.
She took a hard fall on the ice.

senses.head: Definite and based on facts that can be proved
examples: The police have no hard evidence against him.
We need hard numbers, not guesses.

senses.head: Of drinks and drugs: very strong; containing a lot of alcohol, or highly addictive
examples: The bar serves beer and wine but no hard liquor.
He never touched hard drugs.

senses.head: Of water: containing a lot of minerals, so that soap does not lather well
examples: The water here is so hard it leaves spots on the glasses.
Hard water can damage your pipes over time.

entries.takes: to-infinitive, where the subject is what you act on (hard to believe, hard to please); for + person (hard for me); on + person (strict with) or + thing (causing wear: hard on your knees)
entries.contrast: Hard is also an adverb with the same form: work hard (усердно), try hard, It's raining hard. Hardly is a different word meaning 'almost not' (едва): She hardly works is the opposite of She works hard. As with easy, Russian мне трудно is It's hard for me, not I am hard. Hard water has a lot of minerals (жёсткая вода); hard liquor is strong alcohol such as vodka or whiskey, and hard cider is the American name for alcoholic cider. For character, Russian твёрдый is usually firm; a hard person sounds cold and unkind. No hard feelings is 'no resentment', said after an argument or a loss.

examples: The exam was more difficult than I expected.
It's difficult to explain over the phone.
Choosing a college was the most difficult decision of her life.
The family is going through a difficult time.
His question put me in a difficult position.
Stop being difficult and just get in the car.
He can be difficult about money.
She's one of our more difficult clients.

senses.head: Not easy; needing a lot of effort, skill or thought
examples: The exam was more difficult than I expected.
It's difficult to explain over the phone.
Choosing a college was the most difficult decision of her life.

senses.head: Full of problems; causing worry or trouble
examples: The family is going through a difficult time.
His question put me in a difficult position.

senses.head: Of a person: not easy to please or deal with; unwilling to cooperate
examples: Stop being difficult and just get in the car.
He can be difficult about money.
She's one of our more difficult clients.

entries.takes: to-infinitive, where the subject is what you act on (difficult to explain); for + person (difficult for me); about + noun, of a person (making trouble over it)
entries.contrast: Never difficulter: the forms are more difficult and most difficult. Russian мне трудно is It's difficult for me to…, not I am difficult, which means that I am hard to deal with. Russian сложный meaning 'made of many parts' is complicated or complex (a complicated plan), not always difficult. For tasks, everyday American speech prefers hard (a hard test); difficult sounds a little more formal.

examples: It's been a tough year for the business.
The Yankees will be tough to beat.
That was the toughest exam I've ever taken.
She's tougher than she looks.
You have to be tough to survive in this business.
The senator promised to be tough on crime.
Our math teacher was tough but fair.
The city passed tough new rules on short-term rentals.
The steak was overcooked and tough.
Older chickens have tougher meat.
These boots are made of tough leather.
The phone case is made of tough plastic.
He grew up in a tough neighborhood.
He likes to act tough in front of his friends.
"I don't want to go." "Tough. You're going."
Losing your job right before the holidays is tough.
You missed the deadline? Tough luck.

senses.head: Difficult; full of problems or needing a lot of effort
examples: It's been a tough year for the business.
The Yankees will be tough to beat.
That was the toughest exam I've ever taken.

senses.head: Strong and able to deal with pain, hard work or trouble
examples: She's tougher than she looks.
You have to be tough to survive in this business.

senses.head: Strict and firm; not willing to give way
examples: The senator promised to be tough on crime.
Our math teacher was tough but fair.
The city passed tough new rules on short-term rentals.

senses.head: Of food, especially meat: hard to cut or chew
examples: The steak was overcooked and tough.
Older chickens have tougher meat.

senses.head: Of a material: strong and not easily broken or torn
examples: These boots are made of tough leather.
The phone case is made of tough plastic.

senses.head: Of a place or person: rough and likely to be violent
examples: He grew up in a tough neighborhood.
He likes to act tough in front of his friends.

senses.head: Unfortunate or unfair; as Tough! or tough luck, said without sympathy
examples: "I don't want to go." "Tough. You're going."
Losing your job right before the holidays is tough.
You missed the deadline? Tough luck.

entries.takes: to-infinitive, where the subject is what you act on (tough to beat); for + person (tough for her); on + person or problem (strict with: tough on crime; hard for: tough on the kids)
entries.contrast: In American speech tough is the everyday word for 'difficult' (a tough week, a tough call), more common than difficult. Russian жёсткий covers several English words: tough for meat and for strict rules, hard for a surface, harsh for criticism. Tough luck! and Tough! are not sympathy but the opposite: 'too bad, deal with it'. Tough rhymes with stuff; do not confuse it with though or through.

examples: Snow is likely later tonight.
She's likely to win the election.
It's more likely that he just forgot.
We searched every likely hiding place.
The bend in the river looked like a likely spot for trout.
He says the dog ate his homework. A likely story!
"I was at the library all night." "A likely story."

senses.head: Probably going to happen or be true
examples: Snow is likely later tonight.
She's likely to win the election.
It's more likely that he just forgot.

senses.head: Seeming right for a purpose; promising
examples: We searched every likely hiding place.
The bend in the river looked like a likely spot for trout.

senses.head: A likely story: used to say you do not believe what someone has told you
examples: He says the dog ate his homework. A likely story!
"I was at the library all night." "A likely story."

entries.comparison: -er/-est or more/most — more likely, most likely; likelier, likeliest in writing
entries.takes: to-infinitive with a person or thing as subject (She's likely to win); that-clause after it (It's likely that she'll win)
entries.form: -ly from like in its old sense 'similar', so it is an adjective, not a manner adverb
entries.contrast: Although it ends in -ly, likely is an adjective: a likely result, Rain is likely. American English also uses it as an adverb meaning 'probably', usually with most, very or quite or right before the verb: They'll most likely be late, She will likely win. Russian вероятно is safest as probably. Likely allows a personal subject (He is likely to call), but probable does not: say It is probable that he will call, never He is probable to call. Not likely! is a spoken way to say 'no chance'.

examples: He's unlikely to call back before Monday.
It's unlikely that the store is still open.
A deal now seems more unlikely than ever.
The two men formed an unlikely friendship.
She became the unlikeliest of heroes.
The idea came from an unlikely source.

senses.head: Not probably going to happen or be true
examples: He's unlikely to call back before Monday.
It's unlikely that the store is still open.
A deal now seems more unlikely than ever.

senses.head: Not what you would expect; surprising
examples: The two men formed an unlikely friendship.
She became the unlikeliest of heroes.
The idea came from an unlikely source.

entries.comparison: -er/-est or more/most — more unlikely, most unlikely; unlikeliest before a noun
entries.takes: to-infinitive (He's unlikely to call); that-clause after it (It's unlikely that he'll call)
entries.contrast: Unlike likely, unlikely is never an adverb: He probably won't come or He is unlikely to come, not He will unlikely come. Do not confuse it with the preposition unlike (в отличие от): Unlike his brother, he's quiet. Most unlikely can be a true superlative or just mean 'very unlikely' (That's most unlikely).

examples: Will you be able to come on Saturday?
I've never been able to whistle.
With the new software, we're better able to track orders.
She's a very able student.
He was one of the ablest lawyers in the state.

senses.head: able to: having the skill, strength, time or chance to do something
examples: Will you be able to come on Saturday?
I've never been able to whistle.
With the new software, we're better able to track orders.

senses.head: Clever and good at what you do; skilled
examples: She's a very able student.
He was one of the ablest lawyers in the state.

entries.position: both — able to + verb only after a verb; before a noun able means 'skilled': an able student
entries.comparison: -er/-est or more/most — abler, ablest, more able; with to + verb, better able
entries.takes: to-infinitive (required in the 'can' sense: able to swim)
entries.contrast: Be able to fills the gaps where can has no form: will be able to, have been able to, might be able to (never will can). For one success in the past, use was able to or managed to, not could: I was able to get two tickets. Russian способный на + noun or verb is capable of + noun or -ing: capable of lying, not able of lying. The noun is ability; disabled is a different word, about a lasting physical or mental condition.

examples: Are you willing to work weekends?
How much are you willing to pay?
After the strike, management seemed more willing to talk.
There was no shortage of willing volunteers.
She was a willing participant in the experiment.

senses.head: willing to: ready to do something if it is needed or asked; not objecting
examples: Are you willing to work weekends?
How much are you willing to pay?
After the strike, management seemed more willing to talk.

senses.head: Doing something gladly and by choice
examples: There was no shortage of willing volunteers.
She was a willing participant in the experiment.

entries.position: both — with to + verb only after a verb; before a noun it means 'glad to help': a willing helper
entries.takes: to-infinitive (willing to help)
entries.contrast: Willing means you will do it if needed, not that you want to: I'm willing to drive is я не против or я готов, while хочу is want and очень хочу is eager or can't wait. Willing is not a verb form and is not followed by for + verb: willing to help, not willing for helping. God willing is a fixed phrase, если Бог даст.

examples: He was unwilling to talk about what happened.
Many banks are unwilling to lend to new businesses.
Voters seem more unwilling than ever to pay higher taxes.
She became an unwilling celebrity after the video went viral.
The prosecutor called him as an unwilling witness.

senses.head: unwilling to: not ready to do something; refusing
examples: He was unwilling to talk about what happened.
Many banks are unwilling to lend to new businesses.
Voters seem more unwilling than ever to pay higher taxes.

senses.head: Made to do something or be part of something against your will
examples: She became an unwilling celebrity after the video went viral.
The prosecutor called him as an unwilling witness.

entries.position: both — with to + verb only after a verb; before a noun it means 'forced, against your will': an unwilling witness
entries.takes: to-infinitive (unwilling to help)
entries.contrast: Unwilling means you refuse and will not do it; reluctant means you do not want to and hesitate, but may do it in the end. He was unwilling to sign suggests he did not sign; He was reluctant to sign leaves it open. In everyday speech Russian не хочу is I don't want to; unwilling is more formal.

examples: Dinner's ready!
Are you ready for the test tomorrow?
Some kids are readier for kindergarten than others.
She's always ready to help a friend.
I'm not ready to forgive him yet.
By the end of the meeting I was ready to scream.
He looked ready to cry.
I'm ready for bed.
After six months without a break, we're more than ready for a vacation.
He always has a ready excuse.
Students have ready access to computers in the library.

senses.head: Prepared for something; or finished and available to use or eat
examples: Dinner's ready!
Are you ready for the test tomorrow?
Some kids are readier for kindergarten than others.

senses.head: ready to: willing and glad to do something
examples: She's always ready to help a friend.
I'm not ready to forgive him yet.

senses.head: ready to: so upset, tired or excited that you are about to do something
examples: By the end of the meeting I was ready to scream.
He looked ready to cry.

senses.head: ready for: wanting or needing something soon
examples: I'm ready for bed.
After six months without a break, we're more than ready for a vacation.

senses.head: Quick; or easy to get and use when needed
examples: He always has a ready excuse.
Students have ready access to computers in the library.

entries.position: both — in the 'prepared', 'willing' and 'about to' senses usually after a verb; before a noun it can mean 'quick' or 'available': a ready answer, ready cash
entries.comparison: -er/-est or more/most — readier, readiest, more ready
entries.takes: for + noun (prepared for: ready for the test; wanting: ready for bed); to-infinitive (prepared, willing or about to: ready to go, ready to help, ready to cry)
entries.contrast: Ready is not already (уже): Dinner is ready (готов) vs Dinner is already on the table. Russian Готово! about finished work is Done! or All set!. Before a noun the meaning shifts: a ready answer is a quick answer, not a prepared one (that is a canned answer), and ready cash is money you have on hand. The everyday phrase for preparing yourself is get ready: Go get ready for school. Ready-made is a compound: ready-made curtains.

examples: He was reluctant to admit he'd made a mistake.
Young people are more reluctant to buy houses than their parents were.
I was reluctant to leave the kids with a new sitter.
He became a reluctant hero after pulling a child from the river.
She gave a reluctant nod.

senses.head: Not wanting to do something, and slow or hesitant to do it
examples: He was reluctant to admit he'd made a mistake.
Young people are more reluctant to buy houses than their parents were.
I was reluctant to leave the kids with a new sitter.

senses.head: Taking part in something, or given, without real willingness
examples: He became a reluctant hero after pulling a child from the river.
She gave a reluctant nod.

entries.takes: to-infinitive (reluctant to leave)
entries.contrast: Russian неохотно is usually the adverb reluctantly: She agreed reluctantly, not She agreed reluctant. Reluctant means you hesitate and do not want to, but may still do it; unwilling means you will not. It takes a to-infinitive, not about or for + -ing: reluctant to ask, not reluctant for asking.

examples: It's bound to rain the day we go to the beach.
You're bound to feel nervous on your first day.
With so many people involved, there are bound to be mistakes.
The company is legally bound to refund your money.
We're bound by the terms of the contract.
I felt bound to tell her the truth.
The plane was bound for Seattle.
Passengers bound for Newark should change trains here.
Her sense of self is bound up with her job.
The town's history is bound up with the railroad.

senses.head: bound to: certain or very likely to happen or to do something
examples: It's bound to rain the day we go to the beach.
You're bound to feel nervous on your first day.
With so many people involved, there are bound to be mistakes.

senses.head: Required to do something by a law, a promise or duty
examples: The company is legally bound to refund your money.
We're bound by the terms of the contract.
I felt bound to tell her the truth.

senses.head: bound for: traveling toward a place
examples: The plane was bound for Seattle.
Passengers bound for Newark should change trains here.

senses.head: bound up with: closely connected with something
examples: Her sense of self is bound up with her job.
The town's history is bound up with the railroad.

entries.position: predicative only — also after a noun in the 'heading for' sense (a flight bound for Denver); before a noun only in compounds: a Denver-bound flight
entries.takes: to-infinitive (certain to; obliged to); by + noun (a law, promise or contract); for + place (traveling toward); up with or up in + noun (closely connected with)
entries.contrast: Bound to usually means 'certain to', not 'obliged to': He's bound to be late is он наверняка опоздает, not он обязан опоздать. The 'obliged' sense mostly comes with legally, by law, by contract or duty-bound. This bound has nothing to do with the verb and noun bound 'jump' or with out of bounds. The suffix -bound has two meanings: Chicago-bound is heading to Chicago, but snowbound and housebound mean unable to leave. The prisoner was bound is the passive of bind (связан), a verb form.

examples: The baby is due in March.
The next train is due at 6:15.
The report is due to come out next week.
The rent is due on the first of the month.
Your library books are due back on Friday.
She finally got the credit she was due.
The delay was due to bad weather.
Most of the damage was due to water, not fire.
I'm due for a haircut.
After three losing seasons, the team is due for some luck.
Drive with due care on wet roads.
With all due respect, I think you're wrong.
You'll hear from us in due course.

senses.head: Expected or planned to happen or arrive at a certain time
examples: The baby is due in March.
The next train is due at 6:15.
The report is due to come out next week.

senses.head: Owed; that must be paid, returned or handed in by a certain time
examples: The rent is due on the first of the month.
Your library books are due back on Friday.
She finally got the credit she was due.

senses.head: due to: caused by
examples: The delay was due to bad weather.
Most of the damage was due to water, not fire.

senses.head: due for: going to need or get something soon
examples: I'm due for a haircut.
After three losing seasons, the team is due for some luck.

senses.head: Proper and appropriate; as much as is needed
examples: Drive with due care on wet roads.
With all due respect, I think you're wrong.
You'll hear from us in due course.

entries.position: both — the 'proper' sense only before a noun (due care, in due course); the other senses after a verb or noun (The rent is due, the money due to her)
entries.takes: to-infinitive (scheduled to: due to arrive); to + noun (caused by: due to the weather; owed to: the credit due to her); for + noun (going to need soon: due for a checkup)
entries.contrast: Due to has two patterns with different meanings: due to + verb is 'scheduled' (The plane is due to land at six, по расписанию), and due to + noun is 'caused by' (The delay was due to fog, из-за). It does not mean Russian должен in the sense of duty: You are due to pay on Monday means payment is scheduled; for obligation use have to or should. Careful writers keep due to after be and start a sentence with Because of, though Due to the storm, the game was canceled is everywhere in American English. Past due and overdue mean late. The plural noun dues is a membership fee (членские взносы), and in due north the word is an adverb.

examples: He's apt to lose his temper when he's tired.
Cheap shoes are apt to fall apart in the rain.
Shoppers are more apt to buy when prices end in 99 cents.
'Chaos' is an apt description of our first week.
I can't think of a more apt word for it.
She was an apt pupil and learned to read at four.
He proved an apt student of the game.

senses.head: apt to: tending to do something, as a habit or by nature
examples: He's apt to lose his temper when he's tired.
Cheap shoes are apt to fall apart in the rain.
Shoppers are more apt to buy when prices end in 99 cents.

senses.head: Exactly right for the situation; well chosen
examples: 'Chaos' is an apt description of our first week.
I can't think of a more apt word for it.

senses.head: Quick to learn; used mostly in formal or older writing
examples: She was an apt pupil and learned to read at four.
He proved an apt student of the game.

entries.position: both — apt to + verb only after a verb; the 'fitting' sense before or after a noun: an apt description, The name is apt
entries.takes: to-infinitive (apt to forget)
entries.form: from Latin aptus 'fitted', the root of aptitude
entries.contrast: Apt to, likely to, liable to and prone to all mean 'tending to'. Apt to describes a habit or natural tendency (He's apt to exaggerate); liable to and prone to point to something bad; likely to is the neutral, most common choice and can be about a single event (It's likely to rain). In American apartment listings apt. is short for apartment, a different word.

examples: The ice is liable to crack if you walk on it.
Older cars are more liable to break down.
He's liable to say something he'll regret.
The landlord is liable for repairs to the building.
You could be held liable if someone gets hurt on your property.
Violators are liable to a fine of up to $500.
Anyone who lies under oath is liable to prosecution.

senses.head: liable to: likely to do or suffer something bad
examples: The ice is liable to crack if you walk on it.
Older cars are more liable to break down.
He's liable to say something he'll regret.

senses.head: Legally responsible for paying for something or for damage
examples: The landlord is liable for repairs to the building.
You could be held liable if someone gets hurt on your property.

senses.head: liable to + noun: legally subject to a punishment, tax or rule
examples: Violators are liable to a fine of up to $500.
Anyone who lies under oath is liable to prosecution.

entries.position: predicative only — also after a noun (the driver liable for the damage); rare before a noun outside legal writing
entries.takes: to-infinitive (likely to, usually something bad: liable to crack); for + noun (legally responsible for); to + noun (legally subject to: liable to a fine)
entries.contrast: Liable to + verb is for bad or unwanted things (The roof is liable to leak); for neutral or good things use likely to. Liable for is legal responsibility, often with hold (The court held the landlord liable). Do not confuse it with libel (клевета), which sounds almost the same; liable has three syllables, LY-uh-buhl. The noun liability also means a debt in business (обязательство, пассив).

examples: She's prone to migraines.
This part of the coast is prone to flooding.
Teenagers are more prone to take risks than adults.
The paramedics found him lying prone on the kitchen floor.
Do this exercise in a prone position, with your arms at your sides.

senses.head: prone to: likely to suffer from something or to do something bad, often
examples: She's prone to migraines.
This part of the coast is prone to flooding.
Teenagers are more prone to take risks than adults.

senses.head: Lying flat with the face down
examples: The paramedics found him lying prone on the kitchen floor.
Do this exercise in a prone position, with your arms at your sides.

entries.position: both — the 'tending to' sense only after a verb, or before a noun in compounds (accident-prone, an injury-prone player); the 'face down' sense after lie or before a noun (a prone position)
entries.takes: to + noun or -ing (prone to injury, prone to flooding); to-infinitive (prone to exaggerate)
entries.contrast: Prone to is for bad or unwanted tendencies: prone to colds, prone to mistakes; for good ones say inclined to or tend to. Russian склонный к + noun is often prone to + noun, but with a verb English usually prefers tend to: He tends to exaggerate. The hyphenated compounds are very common: accident-prone, earthquake-prone, error-prone. In medical and police language prone is face down and supine is face up.

examples: You're so lucky! You never have to wait in line.
We were lucky with the weather.
I'm the luckiest guy in the world.
It was just a lucky guess.
Getting that job was a lucky break.
It's lucky that nobody was home when the tree fell.
Seven is my lucky number.
He wore his lucky socks to every game.

senses.head: Having good luck; having something good happen by chance
examples: You're so lucky! You never have to wait in line.
We were lucky with the weather.
I'm the luckiest guy in the world.

senses.head: Happening by chance and bringing a good result
examples: It was just a lucky guess.
Getting that job was a lucky break.
It's lucky that nobody was home when the tree fell.

senses.head: Believed to bring good luck
examples: Seven is my lucky number.
He wore his lucky socks to every game.

entries.takes: to-infinitive (lucky to be alive); that-clause (lucky that nobody was hurt); with + noun (lucky with the weather)
entries.contrast: Russian счастливый is two English words: happy for the feeling and lucky for good luck. I'm lucky means удача is on my side, not that I feel joy; a lucky number brings luck. Lucky to + verb often means you escaped something bad (You're lucky to be alive). Lucky you! is envy or teasing, and informal Lucky for you, means luckily. Fortunate is the more formal word.

examples: Is all this paperwork really necessary?
It's necessary to book at least a month in advance.
For a growing kid, sleep is more necessary than homework.
Higher prices are a necessary result of the shortage.
For most people in this town, a car is a necessary evil.

senses.head: Needed; that must be done or had
examples: Is all this paperwork really necessary?
It's necessary to book at least a month in advance.
For a growing kid, sleep is more necessary than homework.

senses.head: Unavoidable; that must happen as a result
examples: Higher prices are a necessary result of the shortage.
For most people in this town, a car is a necessary evil.

entries.takes: to-infinitive after it (It's necessary to book); for + person or thing + to-infinitive (necessary for you to sign); for or to + noun (necessary for growth); that-clause, in formal style with the base verb (necessary that he be told)
entries.contrast: Russian мне необходимо is I need to or It's necessary for me to, never I am necessary, which means that others need me. It takes for, not of: necessary for you to sign. In speech need is far more natural: You need to sign here sounds friendlier than It is necessary for you to sign here. After It is necessary that, formal American English uses the base verb: It's necessary that every form be signed. Spelling: one c, double s. If necessary is a fixed phrase, при необходимости.

examples: It's important to drink plenty of water.
Family has always been very important to her.
The most important thing is that nobody got hurt.
She's an important figure in the state party.
He loves to feel important.

senses.head: Mattering a lot; having a big effect or value
examples: It's important to drink plenty of water.
Family has always been very important to her.
The most important thing is that nobody got hurt.

senses.head: Of a person: powerful or respected, with a lot of influence
examples: She's an important figure in the state party.
He loves to feel important.

entries.takes: to-infinitive after it (It's important to rest); for + person + to-infinitive (important for you to rest); to + person (what they care about); for + noun (good or needed for); that-clause, with the base verb in formal style (important that he be told)
entries.contrast: Two prepositions, two meanings: important to me is what I care about (Family is important to me), important for me is what is good or needed for me (Exercise is important for my back). It takes for, never of: It's important for you to rest, not important of you; of you belongs to adjectives that judge a person's action (kind of you, stupid of you). After It's important that, formal American English uses the base verb: It's important that she take her medicine. Russian важный meaning 'pompous' (важный вид) is self-important or pompous, not important. The most important thing is is a natural way to say главное.

examples: It's vital that she get this message today.
Tourism is vital to the island's economy.
Nothing is more vital to a small business than cash flow.
The bullet missed all his vital organs.
The nurse checked her vital signs every hour.
At 85, she's still a vital, active woman.
After years of decline, downtown feels vital again.

senses.head: Extremely important; necessary for something to succeed or exist
examples: It's vital that she get this message today.
Tourism is vital to the island's economy.
Nothing is more vital to a small business than cash flow.

senses.head: Of the body: needed to stay alive, or showing that a person is alive
examples: The bullet missed all his vital organs.
The nurse checked her vital signs every hour.

senses.head: Full of energy and life
examples: At 85, she's still a vital, active woman.
After years of decline, downtown feels vital again.

entries.takes: to or for + noun (vital to success, vital for health); to-infinitive after it (It's vital to act now); for + person + to-infinitive; that-clause with the base verb (vital that she get the message)
entries.contrast: Vital is stronger than important: without it, something fails or dies. It is usually strengthened with absolutely, not very. After It is vital that, formal American English uses the base verb: It's vital that everyone arrive on time, not arrives; British English often says should arrive. It takes for, never of: vital for you to know. Vital signs are pulse, breathing and blood pressure (жизненные показатели).

entries.meaning: Extremely important, because what happens next depends on it. ---
examples: The next 48 hours will be crucial.
Her testimony was crucial to the case.
This is the most crucial game of the season.
entries.takes: to or for + noun (crucial to the plan); to-infinitive after it (It's crucial to act fast); for + person + to-infinitive; that-clause, with the base verb in formal style (crucial that he be there)
entries.contrast: Crucial means the result depends on it (решающий), which is more than important; it is strengthened with absolutely, not very. After It is crucial that, formal American English uses the base verb: It's crucial that the patient rest. It takes for, not of: crucial for us to win. The middle sound is /ʃ/: KROO-shuhl.

examples: It is imperative that we leave the building now.
It's imperative to keep the wound clean.
Speed is imperative in an emergency.
She spoke in an imperative tone that nobody questioned.
In "Sit down!" the verb is in the imperative mood.

senses.head: Extremely important and urgent; that must be done
examples: It is imperative that we leave the building now.
It's imperative to keep the wound clean.
Speed is imperative in an emergency.

senses.head: Expressing a command: of a voice or tone, or of the verb form used for orders
examples: She spoke in an imperative tone that nobody questioned.
In "Sit down!" the verb is in the imperative mood.

entries.position: both — the 'urgent' sense mostly after it is (It is imperative that…); the 'commanding' sense before a noun (an imperative tone, the imperative mood)
entries.comparison: not gradable — strengthen with absolutely: absolutely imperative
entries.takes: that-clause with the base verb (imperative that he leave); to-infinitive after it (imperative to act); for + person + to-infinitive (imperative for us to leave)
entries.contrast: Imperative is the strongest word in this group and always formal: in speech say We have to or We really need to. After It is imperative that, American English uses the base verb: It is imperative that he be there and that she call us, not is or calls. It takes for, not of: imperative for us to leave. A person cannot be imperative: It is imperative for me, not I am imperative. The noun the imperative is the command form in grammar (повелительное наклонение), and a moral imperative is a duty.

entries.meaning: Sensible and recommended in a particular situation. ---
examples: Reservations are advisable on weekends.
It is advisable to wear a helmet on the mountain trails.
Getting there early is advisable if you want a seat.
entries.position: predicative only — almost always it is advisable to or X is advisable; before a noun say recommended: the recommended dose
entries.takes: to-infinitive after it (It is advisable to book early); for + person + to-infinitive; that-clause, with the base verb in formal style (advisable that guests arrive early)
entries.contrast: Advisable is formal and belongs to notices and instructions (Reservations are advisable); in conversation say It's a good idea to or You should. It describes the action, not the person: It is advisable for you to wait, not You are advisable to wait. Spelling follows the verb advise, with s, not the noun advice.

examples: It's strange that she hasn't called back.
The strangest thing happened on my way to work.
Isn't it strange to see the city so empty?
Never get into a car with a strange man.
It's hard to sleep in a strange bed.
I felt a little strange after taking the pills.
The heat made her feel strange and dizzy.

senses.head: Unusual or surprising; hard to explain
examples: It's strange that she hasn't called back.
The strangest thing happened on my way to work.
Isn't it strange to see the city so empty?

senses.head: Not known or met before; unfamiliar
examples: Never get into a car with a strange man.
It's hard to sleep in a strange bed.

senses.head: Feeling slightly ill, uneasy or not yourself
examples: I felt a little strange after taking the pills.
The heat made her feel strange and dizzy.

entries.takes: that-clause after it (It's strange that she left); to-infinitive after it (strange to see him here); for + person + to-infinitive (unusual for them); to + person (how it seems to them)
entries.contrast: Strange has nothing to do with страна: Russian иностранный is foreign (a foreign language), and a strange country means a weird or unfamiliar one. Stranger is both the comparative and a noun meaning незнакомец: Truth is stranger than fiction vs Don't talk to strangers. Strange to me is how it seems to me (It seems strange to me); strange for her is unusual for her (It's strange for her to be late). It's strange that she should say that, with should, stresses surprise.

examples: It's odd that nobody noticed the door was open.
What an odd thing to say.
I had the oddest dream last night.
Three, five and seven are odd numbers.
The odd pages are on the right.
He built the shed from odd pieces of lumber.
The dish rack was full of odd plates and cups.
He does odd jobs around the neighborhood.
My roommate comes and goes at odd hours.
The house is a hundred-odd years old.
Forty-odd people showed up for the meeting.

senses.head: Strange or unusual
examples: It's odd that nobody noticed the door was open.
What an odd thing to say.
I had the oddest dream last night.

senses.head: Of a number: that cannot be divided exactly by two
examples: Three, five and seven are odd numbers.
The odd pages are on the right.

senses.head: Left over from a pair or set; not matching the rest
examples: He built the shed from odd pieces of lumber.
The dish rack was full of odd plates and cups.

senses.head: Of jobs and times: various and irregular, not fixed or regular
examples: He does odd jobs around the neighborhood.
My roommate comes and goes at odd hours.

senses.head: After a number: a little more than
examples: The house is a hundred-odd years old.
Forty-odd people showed up for the meeting.

entries.position: both — the 'occasional' and 'left over' senses only before a noun (odd jobs); the 'a little more than' sense only after a number, usually with a hyphen (forty-odd)
entries.comparison: -er/-est — odder, oddest; the number senses are not gradable
entries.takes: that-clause after it (It's odd that); to-infinitive after it (odd to hear); for + person + to-infinitive
entries.contrast: Do not confuse odd with the noun odds (шансы): The odds are good. Odd 'strange' is a little milder than strange or weird, and the odd one out is the one that does not fit a group. Odd jobs and at odd hours are common in American English, but the odd beer for 'an occasional beer' and odd socks for mismatched socks sound British. Odd numbers are нечётные, even numbers чётные.

examples: It's obvious that he's not telling the truth.
For obvious reasons, we can't give out his address.
The problem became more obvious after a few weeks.
The twist at the end was a little obvious.
Stop staring at him; you're being so obvious.

senses.head: Easy to see or understand; clear to everyone
examples: It's obvious that he's not telling the truth.
For obvious reasons, we can't give out his address.
The problem became more obvious after a few weeks.

senses.head: Too easy to notice or predict; not subtle or original
examples: The twist at the end was a little obvious.
Stop staring at him; you're being so obvious.

entries.takes: that-clause after it (It's obvious that); to + person (obvious to everyone)
entries.contrast: It is obvious to someone, not for someone: It was obvious to everyone that he was lying. Russian очевидно at the start of a sentence is the adverb obviously or clearly. Said of a person or a joke, obvious is criticism: Don't be so obvious means you are not hiding what you want or think. In state the obvious (говорить очевидное) it works as a noun.

examples: The instructions were short and clear.
The picture on the new TV is much clearer.
Is that clear?
It's clear that she's upset about something.
She was the clear winner.
It became clearer every day that the plan wouldn't work.
I'm not clear about what you want me to do.
Are we clear on who's picking up the kids?
The water was so clear we could see the bottom.
Put your liquids in a clear plastic bag.
It was a cold, clear night.
The forecast calls for clear skies all weekend.
The road is clear of snow now.
Stand clear of the closing doors, please.
Wait until the intersection is clear.
She has beautiful clear skin.
His skin got clearer once he changed his diet.
I need a clear head before I decide.
I have a clear conscience; I didn't do anything wrong.

senses.head: Easy to understand, see or hear
examples: The instructions were short and clear.
The picture on the new TV is much clearer.
Is that clear?

senses.head: Certain; leaving no doubt
examples: It's clear that she's upset about something.
She was the clear winner.
It became clearer every day that the plan wouldn't work.

senses.head: Of a person: sure that you understand something
examples: I'm not clear about what you want me to do.
Are we clear on who's picking up the kids?

senses.head: Easy to see through; transparent
examples: The water was so clear we could see the bottom.
Put your liquids in a clear plastic bag.

senses.head: Of the sky or weather: without clouds, fog or rain
examples: It was a cold, clear night.
The forecast calls for clear skies all weekend.

senses.head: Free from things that block the way; or not touching something
examples: The road is clear of snow now.
Stand clear of the closing doors, please.
Wait until the intersection is clear.

senses.head: Of skin: without spots or pimples
examples: She has beautiful clear skin.
His skin got clearer once he changed his diet.

senses.head: Of the mind or conscience: not confused; not feeling guilty
examples: I need a clear head before I decide.
I have a clear conscience; I didn't do anything wrong.

entries.takes: that-clause after it (It's clear that); to + person (clear to me); about or on + noun (sure about: clear about the rules); of + noun (free of: clear of snow; away from: stand clear of the doors)
entries.contrast: Russian чистый is two words: clean is not dirty, clear is transparent or free of things. Clean water is safe to use; clear water is water you can see through. Clear skin has no pimples, and a clear conscience is чистая совесть. It is clear to someone, not for someone: It's clear to me. Clear is also a verb (clear the table) and, in informal American English, an adverb meaning 'all the way' (clear across the country). The adverb for 'in a clear way' is clearly: Speak clearly.

entries.meaning: Easy to see or understand; clearly shown. ---
examples: It was evident from her face that something was wrong.
His love of music is evident in everything he writes.
The damage was most evident on the north side of the house.
entries.position: both — mostly after a verb (It was evident that…); before a noun it is formal: with evident pleasure
entries.takes: that-clause after it (It was evident that); to + person (evident to everyone); in or from + noun (where it shows: evident in her voice, evident from the data)
entries.contrast: Evident is formal; in speech obvious or clear is more natural. It is evident to someone, not for someone. Do not mix it up with the noun evidence (доказательства, улики), which is uncountable: evidence, not an evidence or evidences. Self-evident means so obvious that no proof is needed. Russian очевидец is eyewitness.

examples: It's perfectly normal to feel nervous before surgery.
Under normal conditions, the drive takes two hours.
After the holidays, the office felt more normal again.
All her test results came back normal.
The ultrasound showed a healthy, normal baby.

senses.head: Usual, ordinary and expected
examples: It's perfectly normal to feel nervous before surgery.
Under normal conditions, the drive takes two hours.
After the holidays, the office felt more normal again.

senses.head: Healthy in body or mind; developing in the expected way
examples: All her test results came back normal.
The ultrasound showed a healthy, normal baby.

entries.takes: for + person or thing, often + to-infinitive (normal for a baby to cry); to-infinitive after it (It's normal to feel nervous)
entries.contrast: Russian нормально as an answer is not normal: to How are you? say Fine, Okay or Not bad. Russian нормальный meaning 'decent, good enough' is decent, good or okay: нормальная зарплата is a decent salary, нормальный парень is a decent guy. In English normal only means 'usual' or 'healthy', and calling a person not normal is an insult. The adverb normally means 'usually'. In above normal and back to normal the word is a noun.

examples: It was very generous of you to pay for dinner.
Her grandparents are generous with their time.
He's the most generous person I know.
The restaurant serves generous portions.
He got a generous offer from a tech company.
The new seats have a more generous amount of legroom.
She was generous in her praise of her rival.
That's a generous way of looking at what he did.

senses.head: Giving money, time or help freely and willingly
examples: It was very generous of you to pay for dinner.
Her grandparents are generous with their time.
He's the most generous person I know.

senses.head: Larger or more than usual
examples: The restaurant serves generous portions.
He got a generous offer from a tech company.
The new seats have a more generous amount of legroom.

senses.head: Kind and fair in judging other people
examples: She was generous in her praise of her rival.
That's a generous way of looking at what he did.

entries.takes: of + person + to-infinitive (generous of you to pay); with + noun (what you give: generous with his time); to or toward + person (who gets it); in + noun (generous in her praise)
entries.contrast: Adjectives that judge someone's action take of, not for: It was generous of you to lend me the car, not generous for you. Compare It was important for you to be there, which states a need, not a judgment. Generous with is what you give (generous with money), generous to is who gets it. The everyday American opposite is cheap or stingy; mean in American English usually means unkind, not жадный.

examples: That was a stupid mistake.
It was stupid of me to leave my phone in the car.
It's the stupidest idea I've ever heard.
I can't get this stupid printer to work.
The stupid car won't start again.

senses.head: Not intelligent; showing poor judgment
examples: That was a stupid mistake.
It was stupid of me to leave my phone in the car.
It's the stupidest idea I've ever heard.

senses.head: Informal: used to show that something annoys you
examples: I can't get this stupid printer to work.
The stupid car won't start again.

entries.comparison: -er/-est or more/most — stupider, stupidest, more stupid
entries.takes: of + person + to-infinitive (stupid of me to forget); to-infinitive (stupid to believe him)
entries.contrast: It takes of, not for, when you judge an action: It was stupid of me to leave the door open, not stupid for me. Calling a person stupid is rude; silly and foolish are softer, and dumb is common in informal American speech. Russian тупой for a knife is dull, not stupid. Both stupider and more stupid are correct.

examples: The test was full of careless mistakes.
It was careless of me to leave the gate open.
I've never met anyone more careless with money.
She moved with careless grace.
He gave a careless shrug.

senses.head: Not paying enough attention, so that mistakes, damage or accidents happen
examples: The test was full of careless mistakes.
It was careless of me to leave the gate open.
I've never met anyone more careless with money.

senses.head: Relaxed and natural; done without effort or worry
examples: She moved with careless grace.
He gave a careless shrug.

entries.takes: with + noun (careless with money); about + noun (careless about details); of + person + to-infinitive (careless of me to lose it)
entries.contrast: Careless is not беззаботный: that is carefree (a carefree summer), a happy word, while careless is criticism (небрежный, неосторожный). Judging an action takes of, not for: It was careless of me to lose the keys. The adverb is carelessly: He drives carelessly, not He drives careless.

examples: My grandmother was a very wise woman.
I came back from that trip older and wiser.
It would be wise to call before you go.
Buying the house before prices rose was a wise move.
It was wise of you to bring an umbrella.
The teachers got wise to his excuses.
Shoppers are wise to that kind of scam now.
Don't get wise with me, young man.
He got wise with the officer and ended up with a bigger ticket.

senses.head: Having good judgment and knowledge from experience
examples: My grandmother was a very wise woman.
I came back from that trip older and wiser.

senses.head: Of an action or choice: sensible and likely to have a good result
examples: It would be wise to call before you go.
Buying the house before prices rose was a wise move.
It was wise of you to bring an umbrella.

senses.head: Informal, wise to: aware of someone's tricks or dishonest plans
examples: The teachers got wise to his excuses.
Shoppers are wise to that kind of scam now.

senses.head: US informal, wise with: rude and disrespectful
examples: Don't get wise with me, young man.
He got wise with the officer and ended up with a bigger ticket.

entries.takes: to-infinitive after it (wise to wait); of + person + to-infinitive (wise of you to call); to + noun (informal, aware of a trick: wise to his lies); with + person (US informal, rude to)
entries.contrast: Russian умный is usually smart; wise means good judgment from experience (мудрый). Judging an action takes of: It was wise of you to wait. None the wiser means not understanding any better (I read the manual and was none the wiser). Get wise to means realize someone is tricking you; get wise with means be rude. A wise guy (a noun) is someone who acts smart in an annoying way, or a mobster. The suffix -wise (clockwise, moneywise) makes adverbs.

examples: It would be foolish to ignore the doctor's advice.
It was foolish of me to believe him.
Driving through a blizzard for a party was the most foolish thing he'd ever done.
I felt foolish when I realized I'd gone to the wrong building.
He looked a little foolish in his brother's suit.

senses.head: Not sensible; showing bad judgment
examples: It would be foolish to ignore the doctor's advice.
It was foolish of me to believe him.
Driving through a blizzard for a party was the most foolish thing he'd ever done.

senses.head: Feeling or looking silly and embarrassed
examples: I felt foolish when I realized I'd gone to the wrong building.
He looked a little foolish in his brother's suit.

entries.takes: to-infinitive after it (foolish to ignore it); of + person + to-infinitive (foolish of me to believe him)
entries.contrast: Here -ish means 'like' (like a fool), not 'somewhat' as in reddish or sixish. Judging an action takes of, not for: It was foolish of me to trust him. Foolish is softer and a bit more formal than stupid; silly is lighter still and often friendly. Feel foolish is to feel embarrassed (чувствовать себя глупо).

examples: Is this the right answer?
"Your name is Sam?" "That's right."
Make sure you have the right address.
You were right about the weather.
She was right to worry about him.
It's not right to take credit for someone else's work.
I hope I did the right thing.
It was right of you to tell me the truth.
He's the right person for the job.
Wait for the right moment to ask.
She writes with her right hand.
Stay in the right lane until the exit.
Something isn't right with the car; it's making a strange noise.
I haven't felt right since the flu.
Check that the corners form a right angle before you nail them.
The two hallways meet at a right angle.

senses.head: Correct or true
examples: Is this the right answer?
"Your name is Sam?" "That's right."
Make sure you have the right address.

senses.head: Of a person: correct in what you think, say or do
examples: You were right about the weather.
She was right to worry about him.

senses.head: Morally good or fair
examples: It's not right to take credit for someone else's work.
I hope I did the right thing.
It was right of you to tell me the truth.

senses.head: Best or most suitable for a situation
examples: He's the right person for the job.
Wait for the right moment to ask.

senses.head: On the side of the body that is toward the east when you face north
examples: She writes with her right hand.
Stay in the right lane until the exit.

senses.head: Healthy, or working as it should
examples: Something isn't right with the car; it's making a strange noise.
I haven't felt right since the flu.

senses.head: In geometry: of an angle, exactly ninety degrees
examples: Check that the corners form a right angle before you nail them.
The two hallways meet at a right angle.

entries.position: both — the side sense and the geometry sense only before a noun (my right hand, a right angle); the sense 'correct in what you think' only after a verb (You're right)
entries.comparison: not gradable — strengthen with exactly, absolutely or just (You're absolutely right)
entries.takes: about + noun (correct about); to-infinitive (right to worry); of + person + to-infinitive (morally right: right of you to tell me); for + person or job (suitable: right for you); with + noun (in order: not right with the car)
entries.contrast: Russian ты прав is You're right, with be, not You have right: have the right to uses the noun (иметь право). Right of you to judges an action (It was right of you to call the police); right for you means suitable (This job isn't right for you). Right is also an adverb (turn right, right now), a noun (human rights, on the right) and a verb (right a wrong). It sounds like write. In geometry Russian прямой угол is a right angle, ninety degrees — never a 'straight' one.

examples: Two of my answers were wrong.
That's the wrong date; the party is on Saturday.
You're wrong about her; she's really nice.
I was wrong to doubt you.
Stealing is wrong.
It was wrong of him to yell at the kids.
We got on the wrong bus.
Sorry, you have the wrong number.
It's the wrong time to ask for a raise.
What's wrong? You look upset.
Something is wrong with my laptop.

senses.head: Not correct or true
examples: Two of my answers were wrong.
That's the wrong date; the party is on Saturday.

senses.head: Of a person: mistaken in what you think or say
examples: You're wrong about her; she's really nice.
I was wrong to doubt you.

senses.head: Morally bad or unfair
examples: Stealing is wrong.
It was wrong of him to yell at the kids.

senses.head: Not the one you need or want; not suitable
examples: We got on the wrong bus.
Sorry, you have the wrong number.
It's the wrong time to ask for a raise.

senses.head: Not working properly; causing a problem
examples: What's wrong? You look upset.
Something is wrong with my laptop.

entries.position: both — the sense 'not working properly' only after a verb (What's wrong?, Something is wrong with it)
entries.comparison: not gradable — strengthen with completely, totally or dead (dead wrong)
entries.takes: about + noun (mistaken about); with + noun (having a problem: wrong with the car); to-infinitive (wrong to lie); of + person + to-infinitive (wrong of him to yell); for + person or job (not suitable)
entries.contrast: Wrong is also an adverb after a verb: go wrong, get it wrong, spell it wrong; the adverb wrongly goes before a past participle (wrongly accused). Russian не тот is the wrong: We took the wrong bus, not We took not that bus, and You have the wrong number is Вы ошиблись номером. What's wrong? is Что случилось?, but What's wrong with you? can sound rude. Judging an action takes of: It was wrong of him to yell.
